bibliography.abstract: Human mobility follows robust statistical laws, but whether these laws persist under large, sudden behavioural shocks remains unclear. Here we analyse privacy-enhanced GPS trajectories of over one million users in California and 180,000 in Massachusetts from January to September 2020, spanning the onset and easing of COVID-19 restrictions. During restrictions, individual ranges contracted below a characteristic scale of about 5 km, while short- and medium-range trip lengths and rare long-distance trips persisted. Exploration slowed from super-diffusive to near-diffusive, and visits concentrated on a few habitual locations. Trajectory shape, once rescaled, was preserved, and the entropy reduction is largely explained by fewer visited locations rather than more regular routines. Recovery after reopening was heterogeneous rather than a uniform return to baseline, and the decline began before mandatory orders. These results suggest that restrictions reorganised, rather than simply rescaled, individual mobility, with implications for mobility-based epidemic models.
bibliography.title: Statistical Laws of Human Mobility under Large-Scale Behavioural Shock

en.caveats: The observed mobility shifts derive from a single disruption event within two US states, which may limit generalizability to distinct shock types or international contexts.
en.what: An analysis of GPS trajectory data from over 1,000,000 users in California and 180,000 in Massachusetts between January and September 2020 revealed that pandemic restrictions altered mobility patterns beyond simple spatial scaling. During lock-downs, individual activity ranges shrank below a 5 km threshold, spatial exploration shifted from super-diffusive to near-diffusive, and entropy decreased primarily due to visiting fewer unique sites rather than establishing stricter visit schedules. Mobility drops began prior to official stay-at-home orders, and post-reopening recovery rates varied significantly across individuals.
en.why: This refutes the assumption that human movement patterns retain their basic statistical properties during severe disruptions, demonstrating that behavioral shocks fundamentally reorganize how individuals explore space and structure daily routines.
